subtopics.title: The Five Number Summary and the Box-and-Whisker

questions.question: For the sorted marks 38, 42, 45, 47, 49, 51, 52, 54, 56, 86, the five number summary is:
The lower quartile of ten sorted values is found as:
options: The average of the second and third values
The median of the bottom five values — here 45
One quarter of the maximum
The third value from the top

questions.question: The interquartile range of the marks is:
The range is a risky spread measure because:
options: It requires the data to be sorted
It is always larger than the median
It cannot be shown on a box plot
It depends entirely on the two most extreme values — one strange mark controls it

questions.question: The deviations of any dataset from its mean always sum to:
options: Zero — the data below the mean balances the data above
The variance
The standard deviation
One

questions.question: For the goals 3, 5, 8, 10, 14 with mean 8, the variance is:
The standard deviation of those goals is:
We report standard deviation rather than variance because:
options: It is always the smaller number
Calculators cannot display variance
The square root returns the measure to the data's own units — goals, not goals squared
Variance only works for even sample sizes

questions.question: Skewness is named after:
options: The hump of the distribution
The largest value
The median bar
The tail — a long right tail is positively skewed

questions.question: For the marks, mean 52 against median 50 signals:
options: Positive skew — the mean has been dragged towards the long right tail
Negative skew — the mean sits below the median
Perfect symmetry
An arithmetic error, since mean and median must be equal

questions.question: On a box plot, positive skew typically shows as:
options: A box with no median bar
Whiskers of exactly equal length
A right whisker much longer than the left — here 32 marks against 7
A median bar outside the box

questions.question: A claim of skewness in an interpretation question must be:
options: Avoided unless the data is symmetric
Justified with evidence — mean against median, or the whisker lengths — in a sentence
Stated using the word 'quality'
Backed by removing the largest value first

questions.question: The outlier fences are placed at:
options: The minimum and maximum
One standard deviation either side of the mean
The class boundaries
Q1 − 1,5 × IQR and Q3 + 1,5 × IQR

questions.question: With Q1 = 45, Q3 = 54 and IQR = 9, the fences stand at:
options: 36 and 63
38 and 86

questions.question: The written verdict on the mark of 86 is:
options: 86 looks too big, so it is probably an outlier
86 is the maximum, so it cannot be tested
86 > 67,5, the upper fence, therefore 86 is an outlier
86 < 67,5, therefore 86 is not an outlier

questions.question: Removing the 86 drops the standard deviation from about 12,5 to about 5,5, showing that:
options: Standard deviation is robust against outliers
The standard deviation is fragile — one value more than doubled the apparent spread
The median must also have halved
The IQR was calculated wrongly

questions.question: In the road picture, the box of the box-and-whisker represents:
options: The stretch between the quarter and three-quarter marks — the ordinary neighbourhood
The whole road from first to last house
The house at the halfway mark only
The two extreme houses

questions.question: On our map, the neighbourhood is 9 marks wide while the right-hand road out runs:
options: 7 marks
13,5 marks
48 marks
32 marks — to the mansion at 86

questions.question: Measuring the road end to end gives the range, which is hostage to:
options: The median bar
The extreme houses — moving one changes the whole answer
The neighbourhood width
The number of houses

questions.question: The interquartile range stays put when extremes change because:
options: It is always equal to 9
It counts every house equally
It measures only the neighbourhood, not the roads out to the edges
It is measured with a longer ruler

questions.question: Averaging the raw distances from the mean, signs included, always gives:
options: Zero — the belows cancel the aboves, because the mean is the balance point
The variance
The interquartile range
A small positive number

questions.question: Squaring the distances before averaging does two jobs:
options: Halves the total and sorts the data
Makes everything positive and punishes big strays more than small ones
Removes the largest value and rounds the rest
Doubles each distance and centres the data

questions.question: The striker's variance of 14,8 must be square-rooted because:
options: 14,8 is too large to report
Roots make the answer more accurate
The five-step recipe always ends in a division
14,8 is in goals squared — a unit no scoreboard shows

questions.question: A rival striker also averaging 8 but with standard deviation 1,5 is the safer pick because:
options: A higher standard deviation means more goals
Her mean must actually be higher
Same average output, far shorter wanderings from home — more consistent
Standard deviation measures shooting accuracy

questions.question: The fences stand at one and a half neighbourhood-widths beyond each end of the box, which here means:
options: At 38 and 86
At 45 and 54
At 50 either side of the median

questions.question: The mansion at 86 hauls the mean from about 48 to 52 because:
options: The mean makes every house share the road's total equally
The mean counts heads down the line
The mansion moves the median first
Means always round upwards

questions.question: The standard deviation reacts even more strongly to the mansion because:
options: It is measured in different units
It only uses the two extreme values
Squaring makes distant houses roar — 86 alone lifts it from about 5,5 to about 12,5
It ignores the houses near the middle

questions.question: With a mansion on the road, the wise report uses:
options: The mean and standard deviation, since they are more precise
The range, since it includes the mansion
No measures at all
The median and interquartile range — robust tools — with a sentence saying why
